problem: Prior VLM-based navigation is object-centric (frontier scoring or detection), needs heavy models or pre-exploration, or depends on detailed instructions or human dialog, so it cannot go to non-object goals such as 'middle of the hall' or 'a corner in the kitchen'.
motivation: Real-world mobility requests are often ambiguous: actions, places or abstract locations rather than detectable objects. A small open-source VLM's commonsense reasoning can provide directional exploration guidance from a bare goal phrase, without environment priors.
key_idea: Use a small open-source VLM as the cognitive core that at every step gives directional text guidance (left/right/forward) and a stop decision. The guidance is rendered onto the image, voxelized with depth into a short-term target area on a top-down map, and reached by FMM path planning.
insight: The ablation shows the VLM decides about 90% of actions over 200 HM3D episodes, with the detection-based frontier backup only about 10%, so the gains come from VLM guidance. Larger VLMs give only marginal gains over the 8B-class MiniCPM (a 30B model lifts HM3D SR from 48.0 to 56.5), so a small model suffices. Real-world ablation: without the VLM, the non-detectable open-language goal fails 0/5, versus 3/5 with it. Failure analysis points to map quality and guidance-to-map projection as the main bottlenecks.
method: Perception prompts: at each step the VLM is asked whether the goal is in front (termination) and, given the RGB view plus a top-down history map, which direction to go for the goal.

Text-to-short-term-target: a summarizer (the same VLM with a different prompt) reduces the answer to left/right/forward, renders the matching image region, lifts it to voxels via depth, and projects it onto the top-down navigation map as the short-term target area.
FMM path planning: an obstacle map built from depth and a fast marching cost to the target area give discrete actions (forward 0.25 m, turn ±30°).
Backup policy: if the VLM output is invalid or says 'explore more', fall back to nearest-frontier exploration with a detector, which can also trigger termination.
Termination: a VLM stop prompt at every step, plus backup-detector termination and a 500-step cap.

setting.backbone: MiniCPM-V 2.6 (frozen), compared with InternVL2.5 series (up to 30B)
setting.model_size: about 8B (MiniCPM-V 2.6); larger InternVL2.5 variants in ablation
setting.action_space: low-level: move forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 30°, stop (real robot: forward 0.5 m, turn 30°)

numbers_note: The split name is not stated in the paper; 'val' is assumed. Ablation figures (parameter scale, VLM involvement) and real-world tables are separate: real-world TV goal SR 80%, SPL 54.1% over 5 episodes; open-language goal 3/5 success.
results: NavVLM reaches the best SPL on Gibson (56.4), HM3D (33.5) and MP3D (27.9), beating VLFM (52.2, 30.4, 17.5) and CoW on MP3D (22.3), with a max of 500 steps. SR is competitive but not best (e.g. Gibson 72.3 vs VLFM 84.0; HM3D 48.0 vs PIRLNav 64.1). Open-goal ability is shown only qualitatively and in a 5-episode real-robot test.
limitations: No benchmark exists for open-goal navigation, so the headline capability is shown only with qualitative episodes and 5 real-world trials.
SR is lower than the best baselines, and performance depends on map quality and on projecting the VLM guidance onto the map (guidance blocked, stop too far).
VLM queries at every step are costly, and the coarse left/right/forward guidance is limited.
